text: Tom offered to feed my cat while I was out of town.
rule: Use 'offered to' + base verb; 'while' introduces a time clause.

text: Tom asked me whether I liked Mary or not.
rule: Use 'whether... or not' to express alternatives; past simple tense.

text: Tom kept on making the same mistake.
rule: Use 'kept on' + verb-ing to indicate repeated actions.

text: Tom really wants to be your friend.
rule: Use 'really' for emphasis; 'wants to be' expresses desire.

text: It's kind of you to say that.
rule: Use 'it's kind of you to' + base verb to express appreciation.

text: Tom asked Mary if he could kiss her.
rule: Use indirect question; 'could' as past tense of 'can' for politeness.

text: It's quite delicious.
rule: Use 'quite' to moderately intensify an adjective.

text: Tom plans to live in Boston for more than a year.
rule: Use 'plans to' + base verb for future intentions; specify duration.

text: There's no place to hide.
rule: Use 'there's' for 'there is'; infinitive 'to hide' indicates purpose.

text: Tom barely made it in time.
rule: Use 'barely' to indicate something happened by a small margin.

text: Don't talk about people behind their backs.
rule: Use idiom 'behind their backs' to mean without their knowledge.

text: Tom decided to tell Mary the truth.
rule: Use 'decided to' + base verb to express a choice.

text: Tom usually sleeps in this room.
rule: Use 'usually' as an adverb of frequency; present simple tense.

text: Tell me why I'm here.
rule: Use imperative mood; 'why I'm here' as a noun clause.

text: Tom knew exactly what Mary meant.
rule: Use 'knew' in past simple; 'exactly' emphasizes precision.

text: Tom pretended that he couldn't speak French.
rule: Use 'pretended that' + clause; 'couldn't' as past ability.

text: Tom promised Mary that he wouldn't be late.
rule: Use 'promised' + object + 'that' + clause; future in the past with 'wouldn't'.

text: Enjoy your vacation.
rule: Use imperative mood for wishes or commands.

text: There used to be a prison here.
rule: Use 'used to' for past states or habits that no longer exist.

text: Keep your hands clean.
rule: Use imperative mood; 'keep' + object + adjective.

text: Tom announced his engagement to Mary.
rule: Use 'announced' + noun; 'engagement to' indicates who he is engaged to.

text: Tom loves talking about politics.
rule: Use 'loves' + verb-ing for interests; 'about' introduces the topic.

text: Tom would like to see you.
rule: Use 'would like to' + base verb for polite requests.

text: Keep an eye on the girls.
rule: Idiom meaning 'watch over'; imperative mood.

text: Let's discuss this over lunch.
rule: Use 'let's' for suggestions; 'over lunch' indicates timing.

text: Tom went to Boston without even telling me he was planning to go there.
rule: Use 'without' + verb-ing; past continuous for ongoing past plans.

text: There's one thing I don't understand.
rule: Use 'there's' for 'there is'; 'I don't understand' as a relative clause.

text: It was pretty expensive.
rule: Use 'pretty' as an adverb meaning 'fairly'; past simple tense.

text: Tell me who I have to talk to.
rule: Use 'tell me' + noun clause; preposition 'to' at the end in informal speech.

text: Tom probably thought I was at school.
rule: Use 'probably' for assumptions; past simple tense.

text: Tom asked Mary which way to turn.
rule: Use 'asked' + object + 'which way to' + base verb for directions.

text: Tom finally got a job.
rule: Use 'finally' to indicate a long-awaited event; past simple tense.

text: Stay away from the fire.
rule: Use imperative mood; 'stay away from' as a warning.

text: This is one of the best schools in the city.
rule: Use 'one of the' + superlative adjective + plural noun.

text: I don't care which choice you make.
rule: Use 'don't care' + question word + clause to express indifference.

text: All you do is criticize others.
rule: Use 'all you do is' + base verb to express habitual actions.

text: Tom asked Mary what kind of movies she liked.
rule: Use indirect question format; past tense 'liked' after 'asked'.

text: Tom was the one who broke the window.
rule: Use relative clause 'who broke the window' to modify 'the one'.

text: Tom wondered who Mary was waiting for.
rule: Use past continuous tense for ongoing past actions; preposition at the end is acceptable in informal English.

text: Let's go and talk to Tom.
rule: Use 'let's' for suggestions; 'go and' connects two actions.

text: Even when she's not wearing makeup, she's very beautiful.
rule: Use 'even when' to introduce a condition; 'makeup' is one word; comma separates clauses.

text: Tom accepted the gift.
rule: Use past simple tense for completed actions; 'accepted' is the past tense of 'accept'.

text: Tom died of old age.
rule: Use past simple tense for past events; 'died of' indicates cause of death.

text: Tom wanted Mary to tell him her phone number.
rule: Use 'want' + object + 'to' + base verb to express desire; indirect object 'him'.

text: Tom abandoned the idea of buying a new truck.
rule: Use 'abandoned' in past tense; 'the idea of' + verb-ing to express a discontinued plan.

text: Tom tried to solve the problem.
rule: Use 'tried to' + base verb to indicate an attempt; past simple tense.

text: Tom borrowed money from Mary.
rule: Use past simple tense; 'borrowed' is the past tense of 'borrow'; 'from' indicates the source.

text: Everyone but Tom laughed.
rule: Use 'but' to mean 'except'; past simple 'laughed' for a completed action.

text: Tom almost forgot to do his homework.
rule: Use 'almost' before the verb to indicate something nearly happened; 'forgot to' + base verb.

text: There's no sign of infection.
rule: Use 'there's' for 'there is'; 'no sign of' means absence of evidence.

text: There is no food.
rule: Use 'there is' to state non-existence; present simple tense for current states.

text: I've been waiting for the bus for three hours.
rule: Use present perfect continuous for actions that started in the past and continue now; 'for' + duration.

text: Tom seemed really confused.
rule: Use past simple 'seemed' for past states; 'really' intensifies 'confused'.

text: Tom went on eating.
rule: Use 'went on' + verb-ing to indicate continuation; past simple tense.

text: Tom likes camping on the beach.
rule: Use 'likes' + verb-ing for general preferences; 'on the beach' specifies location.

text: Get me a towel.
rule: Use imperative mood for commands; 'me' as indirect object.

text: There's room for discussion.
rule: Use 'there's' for 'there is'; 'room for' indicates opportunity or capacity.

text: No matter how much she eats, she never gains weight.
rule: Use 'no matter how much' to express regardless of quantity; present simple for habitual actions.

text: Let's be friends.
rule: Use 'let's' for suggestions; imperative mood to invite friendship.

text: Tom kept me waiting for more than 30 minutes.
rule: Use 'kept' + object + verb-ing to show someone caused another to continue an action; 'more than' indicates duration.

text: It took me three hours to write the letter.
rule: Use 'it took' + person + time + 'to' + base verb to express how long an action lasted.

text: This is quite new to me.
rule: Use 'quite' to mean 'fairly' or 'completely'; 'to me' shows personal relation.

text: Try to read as many books as possible.
rule: Use 'as many... as possible' to encourage maximizing quantity; imperative mood.

text: There's almost no milk left in the glass.
rule: Use 'there's' for 'there is'; 'almost no' indicates scarcity.

text: Tom almost always wears dark clothes.
rule: Use 'almost always' as an adverb of frequency; present simple for habits.

text: It's very dusty in here.
rule: Use 'it's' for 'it is'; 'in here' specifies location; 'very' intensifies 'dusty'.

text: There's only one place Tom is likely to hide.
rule: Use 'there's' for 'there is'; 'is likely to' expresses probability.

text: Remember what I told you.
rule: Use imperative mood; 'what I told you' is a noun clause acting as the object.

text: It's worth talking about.
rule: Use 'it's worth' + verb-ing to indicate that an action has value.

text: Let's go back to the hotel.
rule: Use 'let's' for suggestions; 'go back' is a phrasal verb meaning 'return'.

text: Don't ask me to explain it.
rule: Use 'don't' + base verb for negative commands; 'to explain' is the infinitive form.

text: Let's continue the game after supper.
rule: Use 'let's' for suggestions; 'after supper' specifies when.

text: Tom enjoys watching sports on TV.
rule: Use 'enjoys' + verb-ing for likes; 'on TV' specifies medium.

text: There are a lot of things for us to think about.
rule: Use 'there are' with plural nouns; 'to think about' is an infinitive phrase expressing purpose.
